solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Hospital cover up that may provide a costly lesson

definitions.text: that may provide a costly lesson

indicators.note: up, as in in turmoil or out of order, tells you the letters of the two words before it are mixed

explanation.surface: A hospital hushes something up, and the scandal teaches someone an expensive lesson.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cover up' reads as a single noun, a scandal; split it, and 'up' alone is the signal to rearrange HOSPITAL COVER.
explanation.definitionFit: A fee-charging independent school gives lessons that cost parents money, so its teaching is expensive.

clue.text: Clear passage in Barnet?

parts.note: Barnet is rhyming slang for hair (Barnet Fair), and a clear line combed through the hair is a passage through it

explanation.surface: Someone asks about a road free of traffic in the north London suburb of Barnet.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet is a London borough, but in Cockney rhyming slang 'Barnet Fair' means hair, so the 'clear passage' is the line where hair is combed apart.
explanation.definitionFit: The line on the scalp where hair is divided to each side is a clear strip running through it.

clue.text: Up-to-date training given to hero

indicators.note: training something reshapes it, so the letters of the following words are worked into a new order

explanation.surface: A modern training programme is offered to a hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means fashionable and in tune with current trends, so it matches being modern.

clue.text: Prevent State Department's closure

parts.note: to aver is to state firmly

indicators.note: the closure of a word is its final letter, taken here from Department

explanation.surface: Someone tries to stop a government department from being shut down.
explanation.definitionFit: To ward off or head off something is to stop it from happening, a direct synonym.

clue.text: Quiet Cockney's well-fed, reportedly

indicators.note: reportedly says we hear the words spoken rather than see them written

parts.note: a Cockney drops the H, so 'he's full' (he is well-fed) comes out as 'e's full

explanation.surface: A Londoner announces, in a hushed way, that he has eaten his fill.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney speech drops initial H, so 'he's full' is said ''e's full', which sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word describes something restful and peaceful, so it can stand for calm or untroubled.

clue.text: Tin endlessly filled up with cool round beans

parts.note: a tin is a can

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the trimmed piece reads upwards, from the bottom
without its ends means the first and last letters of the word filled are dropped
round means the word for cool is turned about

parts.note: in, as in fashionable, is cool

explanation.surface: A tin packed up to the brim with chilled round beans.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'up' reads the trimmed word bottom to top. Monk spells the beans with one N, a variant of the usual double-N form.
explanation.definitionFit: These are white Italian kidney beans, so the plural word for pulses describes them.

clue.text: Choose to back first of 26, dropping odds

indicators.note: to back here means to reverse, so the remaining letters are read from the end
dropping the odd-numbered letters, first, third, fifth and seventh, keeps only the even ones

parts.note: the first word of the answer to 26 across is the surname Steptoe

explanation.surface: Someone decides to support the leader of 26, discarding the longshots.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dropping odds' removes S, E, T, E from STEPTOE to leave TPO, and 'to back' reverses that.
explanation.definitionFit: To pick or elect for one option is a plain synonym for choosing.

clue.text: Extend disappointment

definitions.meaning: to lengthen a hem or a rope by releasing it
an anticlimax or failure to meet hopes

explanation.walkthrough: As a verb (let down a hem) it means lengthen; as a noun it means a disappointment.
explanation.definitionFit: Lowering a hem lengthens a garment, and a failure to live up to hopes is a dashed expectation.

clue.text: Marx perhaps worries about Right

indicators.note: about means the word for worries goes around the abbreviation

parts.note: bothers means worries

explanation.surface: Karl Marx frets about the political right.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests Karl Marx; the definition is the Marx comedy family of siblings, with 'perhaps' marking them as an example.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marx comedians Groucho, Harpo, Chico and others were male siblings, an example of the plural word.

clue.text: Write down impression about volunteers

indicators.note: about means the word for impression is placed around the letters for volunteers

parts.note: a note can be an impression or tone, as in a note of anxiety
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve

explanation.surface: Record your impression of the volunteers.
explanation.definitionFit: To set something in written form or symbols is to record it on paper.

clue.text: Obvious, but not very busy

indicators.note: not before the abbreviation says it is to be left out of the word for obvious

parts.note: evident means obvious

explanation.surface: A situation is plain to see, though nobody is especially occupied.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a Scots word meaning diligent; 'not very' tells you to remove V from EVIDENT.
explanation.definitionFit: A Scottish dialect adjective meaning diligent or industrious, so it fits someone hard at work.

clue.text: Receive deliveries earlier than planned?

parts.note: in cricket a team that falls far behind may be made to bat again at once, facing bowled balls sooner than expected

explanation.surface: A customer's parcels arrive ahead of schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket, deliveries are balls bowled; a side well short of the opposition's first-innings total can be made to bat its second innings straight away.
explanation.definitionFit: Being made to bat again immediately means a side faces bowling sooner than its schedule expected.

clue.text: Favours meetings to be arranged after a series of problems

indicators.note: after means the rearranged letters follow the run taken from problems
a series of letters is a consecutive run of them, here a run found inside the word problems, the rest discarded

parts.note: taken as written, only a run in its middle used

indicators.note: to be arranged says the letters of meetings are to be put in a new order

explanation.surface: Favours are granted on condition that meetings be set up after a run of difficulties.
explanation.walkthrough: 'a series of problems' means a run of consecutive letters taken from inside the word, not a sequence of troubles. 'to be arranged' shuffles MEETINGS.
explanation.definitionFit: Kindnesses or good turns done for someone are the plural word meaning favours, chiefly Scots.

clue.text: Almost reach to grab coarse biscuit

indicators.note: to grab means the shortened word closes around the word for coarse
almost means the last letter is cut from the word for reach

parts.note: to gain a place is to reach it
ribald means coarse or vulgar

explanation.surface: Someone nearly stretches far enough to snatch a crude cookie.
explanation.walkthrough: GAIN loses its last letter to give GAI, which then holds RIBALD.
explanation.definitionFit: A British biscuit with a layer of squashed currants, named after the Italian patriot.

clue.text: First to provide housing for initially Utopian, cleaner city

indicators.note: to provide housing for means the word for first goes around the other letters

parts.note: best means first, as in first-rate or top

indicators.note: initially means take only the first letter of Utopian

parts.note: a char, or charwoman, is a British word for a cleaner

explanation.surface: An idealistic cleaner is first in line to be given a home.
explanation.walkthrough: CHAR is short for charwoman, an old British word for a domestic cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of Romania is a European city.

clue.text: Find oneself Liberal, even if nothing else!

parts.note: in old usage 'and' could mean if or even if, as in Shakespeare

explanation.surface: A person discovers they are a liberal, if nothing more.
explanation.walkthrough: The archaic conjunction 'and' (or 'an') means 'if' or 'even if'; 'nothing else' is surface padding.
explanation.definitionFit: To end up somewhere, as in to finish up in trouble, is to arrive or find oneself there.

clue.text: Regularly pay for top coiffure

indicators.note: regularly means take every other letter of the phrase pay for top, starting with the second

explanation.surface: Pay at fixed intervals for a first-class hairdo.
explanation.definitionFit: A rounded, bushy natural hairstyle is a kind of hairdo, which a coiffure is.

clue.text: Message about posh idiot's retracted mistake

indicators.note: about means the word for message goes around the letter for posh

parts.note: a fax is a message sent by phone line
U is the old British label for upper-class usage

indicators.note: retracted means drawn back, so the word for idiot is read in reverse

parts.note: a sap is a fool or idiot

explanation.surface: A note about a posh fool's withdrawn blunder.
explanation.walkthrough: U means upper-class, from the 1950s 'U and non-U' classification of British speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A social blunder or gaffe is an embarrassing error, a type of mistake.

clue.text: Grinding, hard victory in, say, competition when touring

indicators.note: touring means going around, so the word for competition encircles the rest

parts.note: a cup is a competition, such as the FA Cup
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

indicators.note: in means the word for victory sits inside the abbreviation for say

parts.note: EG, for example, is what say means here
a win is a victory

explanation.surface: A tough win in a competition while on tour, for example.
explanation.definitionFit: Chewing something up means crushing it with the teeth, which is a form of grinding.

clue.text: Unititiated soldiers gathered briefly in a group

indicators.note: uninitiated, misprinted in the clue, means without its first letter, so the word for soldiers loses its start

parts.note: men are soldiers, as in officers and men

indicators.note: briefly means cut short, so the last letter of the word for gathered is dropped

parts.note: massed means gathered together

explanation.surface: Raw recruits are assembled for a short time into a unit.
explanation.definitionFit: The French-derived phrase means all together as one body, the same as collectively.

clue.text: Move camera around valley of the piper?

parts.note: to pan is to swing a camera around to follow the action
a dean, or dene, is a narrow wooded valley

explanation.surface: A cameraman sweeps across a valley to find the piper.
explanation.walkthrough: The piper is the god Pan, who played reed pipes; the question mark flags that unusual way of defining the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective relates to the Greek god of shepherds, famed for playing his reed pipes.

clue.text: Half-hearted conflict found in gospel (Mark)

indicators.note: found in means the word for conflict is placed inside the gospel and the letter for Mark

parts.note: Luke is one of the four gospels
war is conflict

explanation.surface: A tepid account of fighting appears in one gospel, according to another.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed 'Mark' looks like a second gospel but gives only the letter M.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally tepid, used figuratively for unenthusiastic or lacking commitment.

clue.text: Note it's to be worn by mafia boss over cape

indicators.note: to be worn by means the note sits inside the boss and the cricket letter, like clothing on a body

parts.note: a don is a Mafia chief
mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale
O is the cricket abbreviation for over

explanation.surface: A musical note is to be pinned on a Mafia chief's cloak.
explanation.walkthrough: O for over is a cricket convention: an over is a set of six balls. 'to be worn by' signals that the note goes inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A loose hooded cloak worn with a mask at masquerades is a kind of cape.

clue.text: Element of body language used by musician

indicators.note: an element of is a part of, so the answer lies inside the words body language

explanation.surface: A gesture that is part of non-verbal communication used by a performer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bob Dylan is a celebrated American singer-songwriter, an example of a musician.

clue.text: Beginning to lose patience, having recently passed? Not according to this

indicators.note: beginning to means take the first letter of each of the words lose and patience

parts.note: late means recently deceased, as in the late king

explanation.surface: A driver who has just passed their test begins to grow impatient.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a learner driver must show this red-on-white sign until they pass the test, so it tells everyone the driver has NOT passed.
explanation.definitionFit: The sign shows a learner driver has yet to pass, contradicting any claim of a recent test pass.

clue.text: Dismiss progressive elements of an extreme crew

indicators.note: progressive signals a step-by-step pick, starting with the opening letter of the word an
elements continues the progression, taking the second letter of the word extreme
of completes the progression, taking the third letter of the word crew

explanation.surface: Sack the forward-thinking members of a radical team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'progressive elements of' takes the first letter of 'an', the second of 'extreme' and the third of 'crew'.
explanation.definitionFit: To sack or fire someone from a job is a common informal sense of the word.

clue.text: Boy wanting to tarry, having run away in German city

indicators.note: wanting here is read as the boy needing something put inside him, so the shortened word goes within

parts.note: a son is a boy

indicators.note: away says the abbreviation for run is taken out

parts.note: to linger is to tarry or stay on
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A boy who'd like to hang about has instead fled to a city in Germany.
explanation.definitionFit: Solingen is a German city in North Rhine-Westphalia, famous for making knives.

clue.text: Totters non-stop, getting teased awfully

indicators.note: awfully means badly done, so the letters of the two words are jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone wobbles constantly while being mercilessly mocked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Totters' looks like a verb; it is a noun. A totter is British slang for a rag-and-bone man, and the BBC sitcom of this name followed a father-and-son pair of them.
explanation.definitionFit: The sitcom's title pair were rag-and-bone men, in British slang called totters.
